prompt: A team runs Trivy on every image in its pipeline. What does that tell it about a virtual machine somebody set up by hand three years ago?

choices.text: Nothing: the machine never went through the pipeline
choices.why: Right. An artefact scanner sees what passes through it; only a scan of the network finds that machine.

choices.text: That it is covered, because Trivy also scans running hosts
choices.why: Trivy reads files; it does not sweep a network for hosts.

choices.text: That it is covered as long as it runs the same base image
choices.why: A shared base image says nothing about what was installed by hand on top of it.

choices.text: That it has the same 162 findings as the image
choices.why: The count belongs to the image the scan read, not to a machine it never saw.

prompt: From outside, linkbox answered `Server: gunicorn`. Why can a scanner that only sees that header not decide whether the service has gunicorn's 2024 advisories?

choices.text: The header is hidden by the security headers lesson 4 added to every response
choices.why: Those headers add policies; they hide nothing, and the server name is in plain sight.

choices.text: Gunicorn hides itself from scanners on purpose
choices.why: It named itself. What it left out was the version.

choices.text: It names no version, so nothing matches an advisory
choices.why: Right. 21.2.0 and 22.0.0 answer the same way; only a reading from inside tells them apart.

choices.text: The advisories apply only to Debian packages
choices.why: They are advisories on gunicorn itself, a Python package.

prompt: Match each question to the family of scanner that answers it.

pairs.right: an artefact scanner, in the pipeline

pairs.left: which port is open that nobody meant to open?
which hosts lack this month's patch?
is the laptop that is never on the office network patched?

prompt: An unauthenticated scan reports an OpenSSH advisory on a Debian host whose package already carries Debian's fix. What produced the false positive?

choices.text: It matched a banner, and Debian backported the fix
choices.why: Right: the banner reads like the old version; the package database would have shown the fixed release.

choices.text: The scanner's plugin feed was weeks out of date on that day
choices.why: An old feed misses new advisories; it does not invent one for a fixed package.

choices.text: Debian publishes no advisories at all for its OpenSSH packages
choices.why: Debian publishes them; that is where the fixed release came from.

choices.text: The host was scanned through an agent
choices.why: An agent reads the package database, which is exactly what avoids this mistake.

prompt: Your company moves its scans from unauthenticated to credentialed. Which new risk does it take on, and must manage?

choices.text: More false positives, because logged-in scans read more files
choices.why: Reading the package database reduces false positives; it is the banner guess that produces them.

choices.text: An account on every host, held by one tool
choices.why: Right. The scanner's credential reaches every machine, so it gets least privilege, a vault and rotation.

choices.text: Hosts nobody listed stop being found
choices.why: The network part of the scan still sweeps the range; it logs in where it can.

choices.text: The scan can only run on Windows
choices.why: Linux hosts are scanned over SSH, Windows hosts through its administrative services.

prompt: Why does an agent work for a cloud instance that lives for one hour, where a weekly network scan does not?

choices.text: Agents are free and scanners are not
choices.why: Both come with the vendor's licence; cost is not the difference.

choices.text: Agents scan the network faster than scanners do
choices.why: An agent does not scan the network at all.

choices.text: A cloud provider forbids network scans
choices.why: Providers publish what may be tested; scanning your own instances is usually covered.

choices.text: It reports from inside the host
choices.why: Right: nothing has to reach it, and the instance may be gone before the next weekly window opens.

prompt: Which of the three products can a student run at home, free, without registering with anybody?

choices.text: Qualys VMDR
choices.why: Qualys is a cloud platform sold by subscription.

choices.text: Nessus Professional
choices.why: Professional is a paid licence per scanner.

choices.text: Greenbone Community Edition
choices.why: Right: open source, free, and documented as a set of containers.

choices.text: Tenable Security Center
choices.why: That is Tenable's management platform for large estates, sold to organisations.

prompt: A friend asks you to "run a quick scan" of the web shop where they work, "just to see". Which conditions must be true before you scan it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Written authorisation from whoever owns the system
choices.why: Yes. A friend who works there is not the owner, and a conversation is not a signed scope.

choices.text: The addresses in scope and the window, written down
choices.why: Yes. A scope says what may be touched and when.

choices.text: A contact who can stop the scan
choices.why: Yes. Some devices fall over when probed, and somebody has to be able to call it off.

choices.text: The shop being public on the internet
choices.why: Being reachable is not permission; that is the mistake the rule exists to stop.

choices.text: The scan being unauthenticated, so that it only reads
choices.why: To the receiving side a sweep looks like the first step of an attack, whatever you meant.

prompt: What is the main difference between running Qualys and running OpenVAS, as their documentation describes them?

choices.text: Only OpenVAS can scan with credentials
choices.why: Both document credentialed scanning.

choices.text: Where the engine and results live
choices.why: Right: Qualys' cloud, or a server of yours. That is the whole appeal of one and the whole objection to it.

choices.text: Only Qualys finds vulnerabilities in Debian packages
choices.why: Both read package databases when they can log in.

choices.text: OpenVAS reads images and Qualys reads hosts
choices.why: OpenVAS is a network and host scanner, like Qualys.

prompt: How many Debian findings did `trivy rootfs` report on the filesystem exported from linkbox's image?
`trivy fs .` on linkbox reports 0 and `trivy image` reports 162. Which reading is right?

choices.text: The image is wrong, because the source is clean
choices.why: The source does not contain the Debian packages, so it cannot vouch for them.

choices.text: They read different files
choices.why: Right: the pins, and the packages of the base image. fs and image are two checks, not one check run twice.

choices.text: fs uses an older database than image
choices.why: Both read the same database in the same run.

choices.text: fs skips HIGH findings by default
choices.why: No mode hides a severity unless told to.

prompt: Somebody applied a Deployment by hand last month, with an image built on a laptop. Which of the checks in this lesson would ever show it?

choices.text: `trivy image` in the pipeline
choices.why: The image never went through the pipeline, so the pipeline never scanned it.

choices.text: `trivy config` on the repository
choices.why: The Deployment is not in the repository; it was applied by hand.

choices.text: `trivy k8s` against the cluster
choices.why: Right. It asks the API what is deployed, whoever deployed it.

choices.text: `trivy sbom` on the SBOM of the last release
choices.why: That SBOM describes the image the pipeline built, not the one from the laptop.

prompt: Put the steps that turn linkbox's image into something `trivy rootfs` can read in order.
`trivy config` flags DS-0002, no `USER` in the Dockerfile, but the image runs as 65532. Why does the check get it wrong?

choices.text: The user is set by the base image, not the file
choices.why: Right, and the check reads only the Dockerfile. The rule is right in general and wrong about this case: a false positive.

choices.text: 65532 is root inside a distroless image
choices.why: Root is user 0; 65532 is the nonroot user.

choices.text: The check reads the build stage, which runs as root
choices.why: It reads the file and finds no USER instruction in any stage.

choices.text: Trivy cannot parse multi-stage Dockerfiles
choices.why: It parsed this one and ran 27 tests on it.

prompt: Of the two ways out of DS-0002, why is adding `USER nonroot` to the final stage the stronger one?

choices.text: It changes the user that the image runs as, from root to nonroot
choices.why: The image already runs as nonroot; the line changes nothing about today's image.

choices.text: It survives a later change to a base that runs as root
choices.why: Right: the file then states the decision instead of inheriting it.

choices.text: An exception would never expire
choices.why: Lesson 7's exceptions carry a date precisely so that they do.

choices.text: Trivy refuses exceptions for HIGH findings
choices.why: Nothing in Trivy refuses that; the choice is the team's.

prompt: KSV-0125 says `localhost:5000` is an untrusted registry. What is that finding, in this project?

choices.text: A defect: the cluster pulls from a registry nobody controls
choices.why: The registry is the project's own, and admission allows nothing else.

choices.text: A sign that the scan could not reach the registry
choices.why: The finding is about the manifest's text, not about a connection.

choices.text: Two policies disagreeing about which registries to trust
choices.why: Right: the check's list and the project's, and the project's is the one the cluster enforces.

choices.text: A low-severity note that can be ignored without a decision
choices.why: It is a medium, and every finding gets a recorded verdict, even "the policy differs".

prompt: For gunicorn 21.2.0, pip-audit's headline said 4 known vulnerabilities. How many distinct advisories were there?
Two scanners report different counts for the same requirements file. What is the first thing to compare?

choices.text: The totals, to see which tool is stricter
choices.why: The totals are exactly what misleads: gunicorn gave 2 and 4 for the same two problems.

choices.text: Each advisory, through its aliases
choices.why: Right. CVE, GHSA and PYSEC names for one problem line up through the aliases.

choices.text: The versions of both tools that ran
choices.why: A version difference can matter, but it is not where two counts of the same file part.

choices.text: How long each of the scans took to run
choices.why: How long a scan took says nothing about what it found.

prompt: A distribution publishes its advisories by ___ package, such as `glibc`, while the scanner meets binary packages such as `libc6`.
A client wants one product to replace both the pipeline's Trivy and the quarterly network scan. What does the lesson say is lost either way?

choices.text: Nothing at all, as long as the product is a commercial one
choices.why: Price does not change where a scanner stands.

choices.text: The view before shipping, or the view of what runs
choices.why: Right. One family reads the artefact before it ships; the other reaches what is already running.

choices.text: Only the format the reports are printed in
choices.why: The difference is in what each one can see, not in how it prints.

choices.text: The credentials, which a pipeline cannot hold
choices.why: Pipelines hold credentials all the time; lesson 17 is about doing it well.

prompt: A credentialed scan of a Kubernetes node comes back clean. What does it say about the packages inside linkbox's image running on that node?

choices.text: That they are clean too, because the node runs them
choices.why: Running them is not the same as recording them; they live in image layers.

choices.text: That they have the node's kernel advisories
choices.why: The node's kernel is the node's; the image carries its own user-space packages.

choices.text: That the image was scanned by the agent
choices.why: An agent reads the host's package database, not each image's.

choices.text: Nothing: they are not in the node's package database
choices.why: Right. That is the question an artefact scanner answers, in the pipeline.
